1.q: Bronwen Hale, the commercial director, is explaining to Larkspur Rail's leadership team why Fair Fares will use agile ways of working. Release 1 is planned to go live in month four so that real usage data from passengers can shape Releases 2 and 3, and nobody yet knows how passengers will react to one-tap claims. Which explanation BEST describes the benefit of working this way on Fair Fares?
o: Adopting Scrum in all three teams will make delivery faster and raise the quality of the app, because the framework sets the pace of the work.
Agreeing the full feature list for all three releases at the start lets the board hold all three teams to a predictable, fixed scope for the ten months.
Short feedback loops from real passenger use let the teams adapt the later releases to what passengers need, cutting work on features of little value.
Releasing early means the board can extend the December end date if passengers ask for more features after Release 1 goes live.
1.w: Agile helps where work is complex and uncertain: rather than hunting for a perfect plan, teams stay adaptable, and feedback loops with continual improvement reduce waste and lead to better solutions (book 2.4, responsiveness and innovation). An early MVP release used by real passengers provides exactly that feedback for Releases 2 and 3.

n.0: This is the classic misconception the book warns against: adopting a framework does not by itself bring faster delivery or higher quality; the value comes from the mindset and culture (book 2.3).
n.1: Fixing every feature up front is the linear approach whose weakness is a lack of adaptability; with this much uncertainty agile favours staying able to pivot (book 2.2, 2.4).
n.3: The board has fixed the end date and budget, and PRINCE2 Agile keeps zero tolerance on time and cost; early feedback reshapes what is delivered, not when (Table 3.1).

1.q: In sprint 3 of stage 2, the Coinbridge Payments developers stop joining the daily stand-ups they share with the app team. Instead they post short written updates when they have time, and two integration problems come to light a week late. Owen Thackeray, the app team's Scrum master, asks how to respond. Which action would restore the agile mindset characteristic that is lacking?
o: Agree with both teams that everyone joins the joint stand-ups, and keep blockers and integration work visible on a shared board.
Let the Coinbridge developers keep posting written updates, and ask Rhys Pengelly to summarize them for the app team every Friday.
Ask Gemma Lowther to remind her developers that the fixed-price contract requires them to deliver the integration on time.
Hold a separate weekly integration meeting for the two team leads, so that the developers can concentrate on building.
1.w: The missing characteristic is transparency and rich communication: information should flow openly, through regular meetings and visible work status, so that obstacles are shared early and without fear (book 2.6.2). Bringing both teams back into the shared stand-up and making blockers visible restores it.

n.1: A weekly summary passed on by the project manager keeps information slow and filtered; it does not restore open, timely and rich communication between the teams (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Contract pressure does nothing to rebuild the open sharing of progress and obstacles that the teams have lost; the gap is in mindset, not in the contract (book 2.6.2).
n.3: This narrows the flow of information to two people and makes it less frequent, which is the opposite of transparency and rich communication across the teams (book 2.6.2).

1.q: During initiation, the Fair Fares project board sets zero tolerance on time and cost for every level of plan but allows the Should have and Could have stories in each release to be flexed. Rhys Pengelly, the project manager, may reprioritize those stories with the product owners without asking the board, and must escalate if the Must haves for a release are forecast to be missed. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Manage by stages, because the board authorizes the work release by release and reviews each one at a stage boundary.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the board has stated who may reprioritize the stories in each team.
Focus on products, because the Must have, Should have and Could have stories describe the products to be delivered.
Manage by exception, because tolerances let the board delegate day-to-day decisions and hear of a forecast breach.
1.w: Manage by exception sets tolerances for the performance aspects and delegates authority within them, with escalation when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. In agile it allows tolerance on what is delivered while restricting time and cost, which empowers teams within control (book 5.2.1.5, Table 5.1).

n.0: Stage-by-stage authorization is not what is described; the board is setting tolerances and the escalation point for flexing scope (book 5.2.1.4, 5.2.1.5).
n.1: Roles are mentioned, but the mechanism is delegated authority within set tolerances with escalation on a forecast breach, which is manage by exception (book 5.2.1.5).
n.2: Prioritized stories make flexing possible, but the decision being made is about tolerances and delegation, not about defining products (book 5.2.1.6, Table 5.1).

1.q: At the project canvas workshop, Bronwen Hale says Fair Fares must at least reach the contract level of 80% of eligible app journeys receiving compensation automatically, to avoid the penalties from January. Any level above 80% would be welcome but is not required. Which performance aspect is she describing, and how should PRINCE2 Agile treat it?
o: Scope, fixed for the Must have stories that produce the 80% level and flexed for the Should and Could haves.
Benefits, fixed at the minimum viable level of 80% and flexed for any improvement above it.
Quality, fixed for the acceptance criteria of the matching model and flexed for the look of the screens.
Sustainability, fixed for the minimum contract criteria and flexed above those criteria.
1.w: A measurable improvement with a minimum the business must reach and room for more is the benefits aspect. PRINCE2 Agile fixes benefits at minimum viability and flexes them above it (book 1.3.2, Table 3.1).

n.0: Scope is what will and will not be delivered (the stories); the 80% is a measurable improvement the business expects, which is a benefit (book 1.3.2).
n.2: Quality covers the characteristics that make products fit for purpose; a target share of compensated journeys is a business improvement, not a product characteristic (book 1.3.2).
n.3: Sustainability concerns the project's impact on the wider environment; the compensation level is a measurable business improvement, so it is the benefits aspect (book 1.3.2, Table 3.1).

1.q: At a board meeting, Dominic Faraday asks why Fair Fares needs organizational change management when the app will do most of the work of paying compensation. Yusuf Bello's 40 staff will move from checking claims by hand to handling unusual cases and possible fraud. Which explanation BEST answers Dominic's question?
o: OCM is a supplier activity that Coinbridge Payments should cover under its fixed-price contract, as its payment service drives the change.
OCM replaces the communication management approach, so that one change plan can hold every message to staff and passengers.
OCM is needed to agree new pay terms with customer relations staff before go-live, as financial reward is what makes a change stick.
The benefits rely on staff adopting new ways of working, so OCM plans the move to the target state and evolves the culture so it lasts.
1.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to a target state (book 4.2.1). Fair Fares only realizes its benefits if customer relations staff work differently, and the change management approach should consider how the culture evolves so changes are not rolled back.

n.0: OCM is how Larkspur itself moves from its current to its target state; it cannot be handed to the payment supplier, whose contract covers building the payment feature (book 4.2.1).
n.1: The communication management approach remains a separate management approach; OCM does not replace it, though communication is one input to how the change is managed (book 4.2.1, 4.4).
n.2: The book points to evolving the culture, not money, compliance or communication alone, as the way to stop changes being rolled back (book 4.2.1).

1.q: Matteo Ricci wants passengers to trust the one-tap claim and, later, payments made without a claim, so that use of the app grows quickly after each release. He asks who should be engaged as a key influencer to shape how regular passengers see the change. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited?
o: Nigel Ormsby, because as passenger panel chair and a daily commuter he has a network and credibility among regular passengers.
Gemma Lowther, because Coinbridge Payments runs the card payments that passengers will receive under the new service.
Bronwen Hale, because as commercial director she holds the budget for customer-facing services and received the mandate for Fair Fares.
Hollie Brennan, because she checks the stories against their acceptance criteria and knows how the claim screens behave.
1.w: Key influencers are people who, through their network, can shape the perception of the majority affected by a change and so most influence adoption and benefits (book 4.2.2). Among regular passengers, the panel chair who commutes daily has that reach; seniority, technical skill or supplier status do not provide it.

n.1: Gemma commits the supplier's staff and owns its contract; she has no network among passengers through which to shape their view of the change (book 4.2.2).
n.2: Seniority and budget make Bronwen a natural project executive, but they do not give her influence over how regular passengers perceive the change (book 4.2.2).
n.3: Technical knowledge of the screens does not make Hollie someone passengers listen to; a key influencer shapes the majority's perception through a network (book 4.2.2).

1.q: In stage 3, the Coinbridge Payments team works from its own offices in another city and follows its own company's ways of working. Its developers are unsure which decisions about the payment screens they can take themselves and which need Larkspur's agreement, and several small questions have waited days for an answer. What should Rhys Pengelly do to lead this cross-organization team MOST effectively?
o: Ask the Coinbridge developers to send every design question to him, so that he can decide each one quickly for both organizations.
Agree clear decision boundaries with Gemma Lowther and the product owners, such as a delegation matrix, for the Coinbridge developers.
Leave each design decision to Coinbridge, as the fixed-price contract makes the supplier responsible for the design of its work.
Require the Coinbridge team to move into Larkspur's offices for the rest of the project, so that questions can be answered face to face.
1.w: When teams work across organizations and cultures, PRINCE2 Agile advises setting clear boundaries within which people can flex, for example a delegation matrix that shows what each party decides or advises on (book 4.3.1, 7.4.3). This lets the Coinbridge developers act quickly within agreed limits.

n.0: Routing every question through the project manager creates a bottleneck and bypasses the product owners; it removes self-management instead of setting boundaries for it (book 4.3.1, 7.3.1).
n.2: Without agreed boundaries, decisions affecting Larkspur's passengers would be made by the supplier alone; the guidance is to define what each party decides or advises on (book 4.3.1).
n.3: Mandating co-location is not the effective answer; teams across organizations and locations need clear boundaries and planned ways of working together (book 4.3.1, 4.3.3).

1.q: From stage 2, the app team works in Larkspur's head office three days a week, the data team works fully remotely, and the Coinbridge team is based in another city. Fatima Zahra says her team feels cut off and hears about decisions late. Which approach is MOST LIKELY to improve communication across this hybrid set-up?
o: Ask each team to send a weekly written status report to Rhys Pengelly, who will circulate a combined summary to all three teams each Monday.
Require all three teams to work at Larkspur's head office five days a week until Release 3 is live, so questions are answered in person.
Agree how information flows between teams, hold in-person days for key people around planning and reviews, and allow informal time online.
Send the same monthly project newsletter to all three teams, so that everyone receives identical messages at the same time.
1.w: Remote and hybrid teams need a more deliberate, structured approach: clarity on how information flows, suitable formats, key relationships, and agreed structured and unstructured time together. Synchronized co-location days for key people help build social cohesion (book 4.3.3, 4.4).

n.0: Periodic reports are not enough on their own and can be biased; they also keep the flow one-way rather than building the relationships a hybrid set-up needs (book 4.4).
n.1: Mandating co-location is not the effective response; hybrid and remote teams need a deliberate, structured approach to working together (book 4.3.3).
n.3: Generic one-way messaging is rarely effective; communication should be two-way and tailored to the groups involved (book 4.4).

1.q: At the starting up workshop, Yusuf Bello warns that paying compensation without a claim could make it easier for people to obtain payments they are not owed. Nothing of this kind has happened yet, but he wants the concern managed throughout the project. Which practice is designed to handle this concern, and why?
o: Issues, because it collects and assesses events that are causing a deviation from what has been agreed.
Risk, because it identifies, assesses and controls uncertain events that could affect the project's objectives.
Quality, because it defines the users' requirements and the acceptance criteria the payment feature must meet.
Business case, because it judges whether the project is and remains desirable, viable and achievable.
1.w: The risk practice identifies, assesses and controls uncertainty so that the project is more likely to meet its objectives; it answers 'what if something unexpected happens, and how do we respond?' (book 10.1). A possible rise in fraud has not happened, so it is a risk to be managed, not an issue.

n.0: The issues practice deals with events that have happened or deviations from the baseline; possible future fraud is an uncertainty, not yet an issue (book 11.1).
n.2: Quality documents what users require and how it will be met; Yusuf's concern is an uncertain future event, which the risk practice handles (book 9.1, 10.1).
n.3: The business case practice keeps the justification under review, and a major risk may appear on the canvas, but identifying, assessing and controlling the uncertainty is the risk practice (book 6.1, 10.1).

1.q: In starting up a project, Bronwen Hale leads the development of the project canvas from the mandate. Release 1, which detects delays and pre-fills a claim for one-tap confirmation, has to be live by the end of month four so that usage data can guide Releases 2 and 3. How should Release 1 be reflected in the project canvas?
o: Show Release 1 as the first benefit of the project, measured by the number of new features passengers can use.
Leave Release 1 out of the canvas and describe it in the team plan that the app team writes for its first sprint.
Record Release 1 as a Could have in the scope section, so that it can be dropped if the budget comes under pressure.
Identify Release 1 as the minimum viable product, so that an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be late.
1.w: Where an MVP is used, the project canvas should identify it so that an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be late (book 6.3.2). Release 1 is described as the MVP and is time-critical because its usage data guides the later releases.

n.0: Features are outputs, not benefits; a benefit is a measurable improvement such as the share of eligible journeys compensated (book 6.3.2, Glossary).
n.1: A team plan is a detailed plan for the next iteration; the canvas itself should identify the MVP so that a forecast delay can be escalated (book 6.3.2, 8.3.2).
n.2: Release 1 is the MVP whose usage data guides Releases 2 and 3; treating it as a Could have would let the core of the project be dropped, and cost has zero tolerance in any case (book 6.3.2, Table 3.1).

1.q: During initiation, Matteo Ricci wants personas to help the teams understand what different passengers need from Fair Fares. A marketing analyst offers eleven profiles based on age band, income and ticket type, already written from survey data. Which approach to personas follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Write up to five fictional, needs-based personas, such as a commuter who uses a screen reader, in a workshop with team members.
Adopt the eleven profiles as written, because survey data on age, income and ticket type gives the most reliable view of passengers.
Build one persona for each member of the passenger panel, using their real names, so that the teams can test directly with them.
Ask the analyst to merge the profiles into five demographic groups and send them to the teams before the first sprint.
1.w: Personas help identify and articulate benefits for users. PRINCE2 Agile advises writing them in a cross-functional workshop with development team members, keeping them fictional, basing them on needs rather than demographics, and using no more than five for new products or pilots (book 6.4.1).

n.1: Demographics such as age and income no longer predict shared needs, and eleven personas is more than the five the book suggests for new products (book 6.4.1).
n.2: Personas should be fictional, which widens the room for innovation, so real panel members' names and profiles should not be used; one persona for each of the panel's 30 members would also be far above the suggested maximum of five (book 6.4.1).
n.3: The number is right, but the personas would still rest on demographics and be written by one person rather than in a cross-functional workshop with team members (book 6.4.1).

1.q: During initiation, Bronwen Hale refines the project canvas. Under expected benefits she lists 'a new compensation feature in the Larkspur app', 'the delay matching model' and 'personalized journey alerts'. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the canvas has to show the main features of the project product so that the board can see what will be delivered.
Yes, because each item can be released early, which lets the benefits management approach plan for early benefits.
No, because these are outputs; the benefits should be measurable improvements, such as the share of eligible journeys compensated.
No, because benefits belong in the benefits management approach and should be left out of the project canvas.
1.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome; an output such as a feature or a model is never a benefit (Glossary, book 6.3.2). The canvas benefits section should list expected, measurable benefits with tolerance, for example the proportion of eligible journeys compensated or fewer staff hours spent checking claims.

n.0: The canvas does show the project product and main features, but in its scope section; listing them as benefits confuses outputs with benefits (book 6.3.2).
n.1: Frequent releases do enable earlier benefits, but that does not turn the released items into benefits; they remain outputs (book 6.3.2).
n.3: The project canvas does include benefits, expected and measurable with tolerance; the benefits management approach covers how they will be managed and reviewed (book 6.3.2).

1.q: In stage 2, Rhys Pengelly needs to forecast which Release 1 stories the app team can complete by the end of month four. The app team's velocity has ranged from 18 to 34 story points per sprint over its last six sprints, while the Coinbridge team reports a steady 40 points per sprint. How should Rhys forecast the app team's progress?
o: Use the Coinbridge team's steady 40 points per sprint, as it is the more reliable figure and story points are shared across teams.
Use the app team's own average velocity from recent sprints, and update the forecast after each sprint as actual figures come in.
Use the app team's highest figure of 34 points, so that the forecast shows what the team can achieve when it is stretched.
Ask the app team to estimate every Release 1 task in hours now and build a fixed plan from those estimates for the release.
1.w: PRINCE2 Agile favours empiricism: start the work, measure how much gets done and forecast from that rate, using the team's own velocity rather than another team's (book 8.3). Velocity is an average rate per timebox and is refined as each sprint adds actual data.

n.0: Velocity should come from the team doing the work; story points are relative to each team, so another team's rate cannot forecast the app team (book 8.3).
n.2: Picking the best sprint produces an optimistic target, not an empirical forecast; velocity is an average rate refined as each sprint adds data (book 8.3, 12.4.3).
n.3: Predicting all the work in detail up front is rationalism; PRINCE2 Agile favours empiricism, measuring the actual rate of work and forecasting from it (book 8.3).

1.q: In the project initiation workshop, the three teams need to break the Fair Fares epics into user stories, group the stories into the three releases and show that payment to the card in Release 2 depends on the matching model. Rhys Pengelly had started a product breakdown structure. Which technique does PRINCE2 Agile recommend for this?
o: Build a user story map from the passengers' activities and turn it into a release map showing the releases and dependencies.
Finish the product breakdown structure first, then turn it into a Gantt chart listing each team's tasks for the ten months.
Draw a cumulative flow diagram of the epics, so that the teams can see which stories belong in which release.
Ask each team to write a team plan covering all its sprints, then combine the three team plans into the project plan.
1.w: PRINCE2 Agile recommends replacing the product breakdown structure with a user story map, built from user activities and broken into stories. Turning the story map into a release map groups the stories into releases and defines the interdependencies (book 8.3.1, 8.3.1.1).

n.1: The book recommends replacing the product breakdown structure with a user story map, and a ten-month task list is not how agile plans are built (book 8.3.1).
n.2: A cumulative flow diagram tracks work items in each workflow state over time to reveal bottlenecks; it does not group stories into releases (book 12.4.2).
n.3: A team plan is a detailed plan for the next iteration, produced when a work package is accepted, not a long-range plan for every sprint (book 8.3.2).

1.q: To satisfy Dominic Faraday, Rhys Pengelly spends the first two weeks of initiation building a detailed Gantt chart that lists every task for all three teams in every sprint up to December. He asks the teams to follow it and to report any task that slips. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a full baseline of tasks lets the board judge progress against an agreed schedule at each stage boundary.
Yes, because time and cost have zero tolerance, so each task has to be fixed in advance to protect the end date.
No, because task-level planning should be done by each team for the next sprint, under a high-level release map.
No, because a Gantt chart should be prepared by project support rather than by the project manager.
1.w: Planning in PRINCE2 Agile is done just in time: a high-level release map at stage boundaries, and task-level planning for the next iteration in managing product delivery, produced by the team in its team plan (book 8.3, 8.3.2).

n.0: Stage boundaries use a high-level release map; a ten-month task baseline cannot hold when the work is uncertain and would be judged on activity rather than delivered value (book 8.3).
n.1: Zero tolerance on time and cost is protected by flexing lower-priority scope, not by fixing every task in advance (Table 3.1, 8.3).
n.3: Who draws the chart is not the problem; the problem is planning every task months ahead instead of just in time (book 8.3).

1.q: At the end of sprint 4, the app team says the 'confirm claim with one tap' story is almost done. The screens work, but the screen reader checks in the team's Definition of Done have not been run. Hollie Brennan, the test automation engineer, asks how the story should be reported. How should the team treat it?
o: Report it as not done and return it to the product backlog, so that Sasha Ellery can reprioritize the remaining work.
Count it as done for the sprint review, as the screens work, and add the screen reader checks as a new story.
Show it as 90% complete on the team dashboard and give it part of its story points in the velocity figure.
Remove the screen reader checks from the Definition of Done for Release 1, so that the story can be accepted now.
1.w: The Definition of Done is a shared agreement on the criteria an item must meet to be complete. An item is either done or not done, with no 'almost done'; unfinished work returns to the backlog for reprioritization (book 9.3.2.2).

n.1: A partly done story may be split only so that the part reported as done meets the Definition of Done; here the screens themselves have not passed the DoD's screen reader checks, so counting them as done hides incomplete work (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: There is no 'almost done' under a Definition of Done: an item is done or not done, and partial credit distorts velocity (book 9.3.2.2).
n.3: The app must meet accessibility standards; weakening the team's agreed DoD to pass a story undermines the quality the passengers need (book 9.3.2.2).

1.q: In starting up a project, Bronwen Hale runs the project canvas workshop for Fair Fares. The participants agree that daily commuters, passengers with a disability or long-term condition, and occasional leisure travellers are the key groups the app must serve, and they rank the three groups in order of importance. Under which topic of the project canvas workshop is this discussed?
o: Persona definition.
User group definition.
Benefits analysis.
Business value definition.
1.w: In the project canvas workshop, the user group definition topic identifies one to three key user groups and prioritizes them (book 13.2.4.1, Table 13.2). Persona definition comes later, in the project initiation workshop.

n.0: Personas are defined in the project initiation workshop during initiation; the canvas workshop identifies and ranks the key user groups (Table 13.7, Table 13.2).
n.2: Benefits analysis identifies benefits and dis-benefits and their tolerances, not which user groups matter most (Table 13.2).
n.3: Business value definition concerns the value the project brings to the organization, not the identification and ranking of user groups (Table 13.2).

1.q: After the mandate is issued, Rhys Pengelly works with Matteo Ricci, Gemma Lowther and Bronwen Hale to agree what Fair Fares will deliver, and creates the project backlog with epics for delay detection, payment and alerts. At the same time, Bronwen leads work on the project canvas. Which activity of the 'starting up a project' process is this, and why?
o: Select the project approach, as the team is deciding how the epics will be delivered by the three teams.
Assemble the project brief, as the scope and exclusions of the project are being confirmed for the board.
Plan the initiation stage, as the epics will be refined further while the project is being initiated.
Prepare the outline business case, as the project canvas and the project backlog are drafted in it.
1.w: In PRINCE2 Agile's version of 'prepare the outline business case', the project executive leads the project canvas from the mandate, and the project manager, with the CPO, senior supplier and executive, defines what is to be delivered and creates the project backlog (book Table 13.1).

n.0: Selecting the project approach evaluates delivery solutions and tailoring needs; drafting the canvas and creating the project backlog belong to preparing the outline business case (Table 13.1).
n.1: Assembling the brief confirms objectives, scope, tolerances, constraints and dependencies once the outline business case exists; it is not where the canvas and backlog are first drafted (Table 13.1).
n.2: Planning the initiation stage sets the constraints, release map and controls for initiation; it does not cover defining the deliverables or the canvas (Table 13.1).

1.q: In stage 2, the project board, Priyanka Desai and two business representatives hold an agile enablement workshop. They have already agreed that resistance in customer relations is the most serious threat to agile adoption, and they now agree practical actions, such as inviting Yusuf Bello's supervisors to each product demo. Under which topic of the workshop is this done?
o: Risk planning.
Agilometer assessment review.
Risk identification.
Risk assessment.
1.w: The agile enablement workshop moves through Agilometer assessment review, risk identification, risk assessment and risk planning, where practical mitigation steps are agreed (book Table 13.5). The risk has already been prioritized, so agreeing actions is risk planning.

n.1: This topic links the Agilometer's risk areas to agile values and transformation objectives to build a shared view of key risks; it precedes the planning of actions (Table 13.5).
n.2: Risk identification looks for further agile-adoption threats and opportunities; this risk has already been identified (Table 13.5).
n.3: Risk assessment estimates probability and impact and prioritizes; the group has already ranked this risk and is now deciding responses (Table 13.5).

1.q: Midway through stage 3, Rhys Pengelly asks Bronwen Hale whether passengers with paper season tickets should be included in Release 2. The question is outside his authority but does not threaten any tolerance. Bronwen discusses it with the other board members by phone and gives him an answer the next day. Which activity of the 'directing a project' process is this?
o: Authorize a stage or exception plan.
Authorize the project.
Give ongoing direction.
Authorize initiation.
1.w: 'Give ongoing direction' covers the board's informal guidance at any time, in response to informal requests, business advice, escalated issues and exception reports (book Table 13.4). Bronwen is answering an informal request without approving any plan.

n.0: This activity approves an updated release map for the next stage or an exception plan; no plan is being approved here (Table 13.4).
n.1: Authorizing the project approves the PID and commits resources at the end of initiation; the project is already in stage 3 (Table 13.4).
n.3: Authorizing initiation approves the project brief and release map for initiation at the start of the project, long before stage 3 (Table 13.4).

2.q: At a council meeting, Professor Alison Greer is asked why the Student Support Hub will be delivered with agile ways of working instead of one full design approved at the start. Demand has risen by 60% in four years, the wellbeing service is still working out how it will triage requests, and nobody is sure how students will prefer to ask for help. Which explanation BEST reflects why agile suits this project?
o: Adopting Scrum in both teams will make delivery faster and raise quality, whatever ways of working the wellbeing service keeps.
Agile lets the university fix every feature of the hub now and flex the budget and the go-live date as needs become clearer.
The right solution is uncertain, so short feedback loops with students and staff let the teams adapt quickly and reduce wasted work.
Agile lets the teams start building before the business justification is agreed, which saves time against the Welcome Week deadline.
2.w: Complex situations rarely have one perfect solution known at the start, so it is better to stay adaptable and able to pivot quickly. Feedback loops and continual improvement reduce waste and give better solutions to complex problems (book 2.4). Here the triage model and students' preferences are both uncertain.

n.0: This is the classic misconception: adopting a framework does not by itself bring faster delivery or higher quality; the value comes from a change in mindset and culture (book 2.3).
n.1: PRINCE2 Agile does the reverse: time and cost are fixed with zero tolerance, and what is delivered is flexed (book Table 3.1). The council has also said the budget is fixed.
n.3: Every PRINCE2 Agile project still needs business justification; it is tailored into a project canvas, not dropped (book 5.2.1.1, 6.3.1).

2.q: To prepare for the new hub, managers in the wellbeing service introduce a daily stand-up and a wall board of sticky notes for the triage redesign. However, every change to a triage step still needs written sign-off from a senior manager, and advisers are told to follow the new routine exactly as set out. Dr Kwame Mensah asks Jamal Hussain how this looks from an agile point of view. Which statement BEST describes the situation?
o: The service is doing agile without being agile: it has adopted agile routines, but staff are not allowed to adapt and decide for themselves.
The service is being agile, because daily stand-ups and a visible wall board show that the agile mindset is already in place among wellbeing staff.
The service is being agile without doing agile, because it has the right mindset but has not yet adopted a framework such as Scrum.
The service is both being and doing agile, because senior sign-off keeps each change within the tolerances agreed with the board.
2.w: Doing agile is the practical use of agile frameworks, techniques and terms; being agile means thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply that mindset with suitable self-management (book 2.3.1). Stand-ups and boards with rigid sign-off and fixed routines are doing agile without being agile.

n.1: Stand-ups and boards are visible practices; they do not show the mindset when staff cannot adapt or decide anything for themselves (book 2.3.1, 2.6.1).
n.2: The reverse is true: the service has adopted agile routines (doing) but restricts the freedom to think and act in an agile way (being) (book 2.3.1).
n.3: Tolerances are set for the project, not for every triage step; requiring senior sign-off for each change removes the self-management that being agile needs (book 2.3.1, Table 5.1).

2.q: In starting up a project, Jamal Hussain hears that wellbeing staff have seen three previous systems promised and then dropped. Before planning the initiation stage, he meets Tom Brierley and two other advisers to find out why those systems failed, and records what they say so that the Student Support Hub can act on it. Which principle is Jamal applying, and why?
o: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because he is engaging internal stakeholders who will use the hub.
Ensure continued business justification, because past failures show whether the hub is likely to be worthwhile.
Tailor to suit the project, because he is adapting the method to the culture of the wellbeing service.
Learn from experience, because he is seeking lessons from earlier initiatives at the start and using them in the project.
2.w: Learning from experience means seeking, recording and acting on lessons throughout the project, starting with lessons from previous similar work in starting up (book 5.2, Table 5.1; assess previous lessons, Table 13.1). Jamal is gathering lessons from the three earlier systems.

n.0: Engaging stakeholders is part of defining roles and relationships, but Jamal's purpose here is to capture why earlier systems failed, which is learning from experience (book 5.2.1.3).
n.1: Continued business justification keeps checking that the project is desirable, viable and achievable; the stem describes gathering lessons, not reviewing justification (book 5.2.1.1).
n.2: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's size, complexity and context; Jamal has not changed how the method is applied, he has collected lessons (book 5.2.1.7).

2.q: Midway through stage 2, the Release 1 burn-up chart shows that the web team will finish self-referral and booking before Welcome Week, but not the full self-help content library or a live chat option, both rated Should or Could haves. Professor Greer has said self-referral and booking are the minimum for Welcome Week, and the council has fixed the budget. Which response BEST applies PRINCE2 Agile fix and flex?
o: Move Release 1 to two weeks after Welcome Week, so that every planned feature can go live together for new students.
Keep the date and budget, launch self-referral and booking, and move the unfinished Should and Could haves to Release 2.
Drop booking from Release 1 and finish the self-help library instead, as the library costs less to complete in the time left.
Ask the council for extra funding to hire contract developers, so that the full Release 1 scope is ready for Welcome Week.
2.w: PRINCE2 Agile fixes time and cost with zero tolerance and flexes scope: Must haves are fixed and Should and Could haves are flexed (book Table 3.1). Self-referral and booking are the stated minimum, so they go live on time and the lower-priority features move to a later release.

n.0: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan; delaying Release 1 past Welcome Week to protect lower-priority scope breaks the fixed date (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Booking is part of the minimum the university must offer, so it is a Must have and fixed; it cannot be traded for a lower-priority feature (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Cost has zero tolerance and the council has fixed the budget; extra funding to protect Should and Could haves flexes the wrong aspect (book Table 3.1).

2.q: Before Release 1, the university plans to send the 45 wellbeing staff a user guide and a recorded webinar on the new triage process, and then let them get on with it. Several staff have already said they feel the change is being done to them, and some have seen earlier systems dropped. Which action is MOST LIKELY to help staff adopt the new ways of working?
o: Send the guide and webinar as planned, and ask managers to report which staff have watched the webinar by the go-live date.
Train the senior managers in depth and ask them to pass the details on to their teams once Release 1 is live.
Combine short training with on-the-job coaching for staff in their own teams, planned to match each release of the hub.
Give staff early access to the case management tool first, so that they learn the new ways of working by using it.
2.w: People need theoretical training and practical on-the-job coaching to understand how changes apply to them; informing people and leaving them to cope breeds frustration, a leading cause of resistance. PRINCE2 Agile suggests a training and coaching plan mapped to the stages of the change (book 2.7.3).

n.0: This is informing people and leaving them to fend for themselves; tracking who watched a webinar measures compliance, not understanding (book 2.7.3).
n.1: As many people as possible should understand what is changing and why; limiting training to managers and passing details on later leaves staff unsupported at go-live (book 2.7.3).
n.3: Introducing a tool first does not build the knowledge and skills people need; training and coaching should come first (book 2.7.3).

2.q: At a project board meeting, a council member asks why the Student Support Hub needs organizational change management. In her view, the web team and Northmere will build the hub, and once it is live the wellbeing staff will simply have to use it. Which explanation BEST answers her question?
o: OCM gives the board a way to instruct staff to use the hub by a set date, and clear instructions with a deadline are what make staff comply.
OCM is needed because the change management approach cannot be used outside a project, so another discipline must cover the wellbeing service's 45 staff.
OCM is mostly a record of the training given, because frequent releases of the hub are what make staff adopt the new ways of working.
The service must move from its current way of triaging to a new target state, and the change lasts if the culture adopts it rather than rolling back.
2.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to the target state (book 4.2.1). Building the hub does not change how 45 staff triage requests; the culture has to evolve so that the change is not rolled back once the project ends (book 4.2.1, 4.2.3).

n.0: Making change stick depends on evolving the culture, not on compliance with instructions; staff who have seen three systems dropped are unlikely to adopt the hub because of a deadline (book 4.2.1).
n.1: The change management approach can be tailored for use outside a project, for example to describe the target state for the business (book 4.2.1, Table 4.1).
n.2: Frequent releases support adoption, but OCM is the whole transition from current to target state, including culture and communication, not a training record (book 4.2.1, 4.2.4).

2.q: Dr Kwame Mensah wants the wellbeing staff to adopt the new triage process before Welcome Week. Many staff fear that a digital route will make support feel impersonal, and some doubt the hub will last. Jamal Hussain asks who should be engaged as a key influencer to shape how the staff see the change. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited, and why?
o: Dr Kwame Mensah, because as director of the service he has the authority to require staff to use the new process.
Tom Brierley, because he is respected by his colleagues, so his views can shape how many staff see the hub.
Ian Prothero, because Northmere supplies the records system and can explain how the link to the hub will work.
Dr Ruth Sefton, because she must approve the handling of health data and can reassure staff that it is secure.
2.w: A key influencer is someone who can shape the perception of the majority and, through their network, most affect the adoption of the change (book 4.2.2). Tom Brierley is respected by the staff who must change, and his open doubts mean his support would carry weight with colleagues who share them.

n.0: Formal authority is not the same as influence over colleagues' perceptions; the key influencer is the person with network and credibility among those affected (book 4.2.2).
n.2: Ian Prothero is the supplier's account manager; he has no network among the wellbeing staff whose adoption matters (book 4.2.2).
n.3: Dr Sefton is a specialist approver; reassurance on data is useful, but she does not have the peer network that shapes how staff see the change (book 4.2.2).

2.q: In stage 2, the Northmere developers work from their own offices under their company's rules, while the university web team works on campus. The two teams must agree how the hub exchanges data with the records system, but they have never met, and misunderstandings over the shared data fields have already cost a sprint. Which action BEST builds the working relationship between the two teams?
o: Agree regular days when key people from both teams work together in person, and set aside online time for less structured conversation.
Require all the Northmere developers to work on campus every day until Release 1 is live, so that the teams can share one room.
Limit contact between the teams to written requests passed through Jamal Hussain, so that the per-iteration agreement with Northmere is protected.
Leave the two teams to build their own relationship, as self-managing teams decide for themselves how they will work together.
2.w: Teams that work apart need a plan for how they will use their time together and build social cohesion. Sync co-location days for key people and teams, plus time for less structured conversation online, are the aids PRINCE2 Agile suggests (book 4.3.3).

n.1: Mandating full co-location for another organization's staff is not the effective answer; planned co-location days for key people build cohesion without it (book 4.3.3).
n.2: Channelling all contact through the project manager reduces collaboration and rich communication, which is what caused the misunderstandings (book 4.3.3, 4.4).
n.3: Self-management works within clear boundaries; leading teams across organizations means planning how people work together, not leaving it to chance (book 4.3.1, 4.3.3).

2.q: The wellbeing staff work across both campuses, and many work part-time or remotely, so they often miss face-to-face meetings about the new triage process. Jamal Hussain is drafting the communication management approach and asks how communication should be handled for this group. Which explanation BEST fits PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Hold all briefings in person on the main campus, because rich communication needs people to be in the same room together.
Send one weekly email to all 45 staff, because a single message for everyone keeps the information on the change consistent.
Plan a deliberate structure: agreed formats and channels, the key relationships, and set times for structured and informal contact.
Rely on a formal monthly report to the service, because informal conversations about the change cannot be controlled by the project.
2.w: Remote and hybrid working need a more deliberate, structured approach to communication: clarity on how information flows and in which formats, the key relationships, and agreed structured and unstructured time together (book 4.4). This group works in a hybrid way across two campuses.

n.0: Rich communication is not limited to face-to-face meetings, and in-person briefings would keep excluding the part-time and remote staff who already miss meetings (book 4.4).
n.1: Generic one-way messaging is rarely effective; communication should be bidirectional and tailored to groups, with listening as well as broadcasting (book 4.4).
n.3: Most communication happens outside formal channels and should be accepted and supported; periodic reports on their own are not enough (book 4.4).

2.q: For Release 1, Dr Kwame Mensah forms a triage team of eight advisers from both campuses to handle self-referrals. They have not worked together before, and several are unsure which changes to the triage questions they may make themselves and which need his approval. Which action BEST helps build this into an agile team?
o: Kwame writes the team's values and decision rules himself and circulates them, so that the advisers can start triaging without delay.
Pay a monthly bonus to the advisers who close the most self-referral requests, so that the team is motivated to work quickly.
Ask each adviser to email Kwame a daily summary, so that he can approve any change to the triage questions before it is made.
Hold a session where the team co-decides its values and agrees which decisions it can take and which must be escalated.
2.w: Building agile teams starts with co-deciding team values and accountabilities, so that the team knows the boundaries of its self-management and when decisions must be escalated (book 4.5).

n.0: Values and accountabilities should be co-decided by the team; values written by a manager do not build shared ownership (book 4.5).
n.1: PRINCE2 Agile suggests value-based incentives that reward behaviour modelling agile values, balanced with intangible motivators; a bonus for volume can reward rushing urgent cases (book 4.5).
n.2: Approving every change centrally removes self-management; the team needs agreed boundaries, not daily approval (book 4.5).

2.q: During initiation, the university's quality team asks for evidence that each release of the Student Support Hub has been tested with real students, and the hub must work with screen readers. Jamal Hussain wants to settle what the users will accept and how that will be checked. Which practice addresses this concern, and why?
o: Quality, because it documents the users' requirements of the project products and how they will be met.
Progress, because it monitors actual achievements against those planned and forecasts the project's objectives.
Risk, because failing an accessibility check is an uncertain event that could affect the project's objectives.
Issues, because a release that has not been tested with students will deviate from the agreed baseline.
2.w: The quality practice documents the users' requirements of the project products and establishes how they will be met; it answers 'what is acceptable to users and how is it measured?' (book 9.1). Accessibility standards and testing with students are quality requirements and quality methods.

n.1: Progress compares actual achievements with plans and forecasts objectives; it does not define what users will accept or how products are checked (book 12.1).
n.2: A failed check is a possible threat, but defining acceptable quality and how it is verified is the quality practice, not the risk practice (book 9.1, 10.1).
n.3: Nothing has deviated yet; the issues practice controls changes to the baseline, while the quality team's request is about defining and meeting requirements (book 9.1, 11.1).

2.q: Jamal Hussain is drafting the benefits management approach. Professor Greer wants evidence of benefits, such as fewer paper forms printed and shorter waits for a first appointment, well before the project closes in month 14. How should the approach reflect this?
o: Plan a single benefits review after the project closes, because benefits cannot be realized until all three releases are live.
Treat the on-time go-live of each release as the benefit, because meeting each date shows that value has been delivered.
Leave benefits out of the approach until Release 3, because the early-warning feature is expected to bring the largest benefit to students.
Use the releases to deliver benefits early, and set out when and how each benefit will be measured and reviewed after each release.
2.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the benefits management approach plans frequent releases so that benefits can be delivered early, and it sets out how benefits will be measured, reviewed and by whom (book 6.3.2). Iterative releases can realize some benefits during the project, not only after closure (book 6.3.1).

n.0: Most benefit confirmation happens after closure, but iterative releases let some benefits be realized and measured during the project (book 6.3.1).
n.1: A go-live date is a time target and a release is an output; a benefit is a measurable improvement such as shorter waiting times (book 6.3.2, Glossary).
n.2: Release 3 may not be built at all, subject to ethics review; Releases 1 and 2 already bring measurable benefits that the approach should plan for (book 6.3.2).

2.q: In starting up a project, Jamal Hussain assembles the project brief for the Student Support Hub. Professor Greer wants the brief to show clearly how the agile approach will shape the project, as most university leaders are used to annual plans. Which content is MOST appropriate to add to the brief?
o: A fixed list of every feature in all three releases, so that the council can approve the whole scope before initiation starts.
The scope and quality areas that can flex by priority, the agile techniques chosen and their benefits, and how releases affect operations.
The web team's task plans for its first three sprints, so that the board can approve the work each developer will do on the hub in stage 2.
The design of the web team's online dashboard, so that the board can see how sprint progress will be reported to it each week.
2.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the project brief outlines the flexible areas of scope and quality criteria based on prioritization, the agile techniques and approaches chosen with their expected benefits, and, because of incremental delivery, more detail on the impact on operations and maintenance (book 6.3.2).

n.0: Fixing every feature in advance removes the flexibility on scope that agile relies on; Must haves are fixed but Should and Could haves flex (book 6.3.2, Table 3.1).
n.2: Task-level plans are produced by the team for the next iteration in managing product delivery, not by the board in starting up (book 8.3.2).
n.3: Team dashboards are co-created by each team in the project kickoff workshop; the board pulls information from the project dashboard (book Table 13.8, Table 12.1).

2.q: During initiation, Professor Greer refines the project canvas. It shows one cost figure of £950,000 and one forecast of benefits, which assumes that all three releases, including the early-warning feature, will be delivered. The ethics committee has not yet reviewed the early-warning feature. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the budget is fixed, so a single cost figure and a single benefits forecast give the board all it needs.
Yes, because the canvas is a one-page summary, so alternative outcomes should be kept for the full business case.
No, because the canvas should show best-case, worst-case and expected-case scenarios, such as benefits without Release 3.
No, because benefits belong in the benefits management approach and should not be forecast on the project canvas.
2.w: When the business case is tailored into a project canvas, the canvas should outline best-case, worst-case and expected-case scenarios (book Table 5.2). Release 3 depends on an ethics review, so the board needs to see whether the hub is still justified if it is not built.

n.0: A fixed budget does not remove uncertainty about benefits; the forecast depends on a feature that may never be approved (book Table 5.2).
n.1: The canvas is a one-page visual business justification, and in PRINCE2 Agile it is the business case; it should still outline the different scenarios (book 6.3.2, Table 5.2).
n.3: The project canvas includes expected, measurable benefits with tolerance; the benefits management approach covers how they will be managed and reviewed (book 6.3.2).

2.q: Early in stage 2, Northmere developers change two shared data fields without telling the web team, while web developers wait for approvals they do not need. Jamal Hussain wants to make clear, for each type of decision about the link to the records system, who decides and who must be involved, such as Rebecca Lyle or Dr Ruth Sefton. Which technique should he use?
o: A team skill matrix, showing each developer's strengths and gaps on the two team dashboards.
The commercial management approach, setting out the delivery model for Northmere's work.
A delegation matrix, showing for each decision area who decides and who is involved.
A user story map, showing the order in which the integration stories will be delivered.
2.w: A delegation matrix makes responsibilities and decision authority transparent: for each decision area it shows who decides and who is involved (book 7.4.3). Here both teams are unsure which decisions they can take.

n.0: A team skill matrix shows capabilities, strengths and gaps to assign people and plan training; it does not set decision authority (book 7.4.1).
n.1: The commercial management approach covers procurement and contract arrangements, such as the per-iteration payment, not who decides each technical question (book 7.3.2).
n.3: A story map breaks products into user stories and orders them; it does not make decision rights clear (book 8.3.2.4).

2.q: During initiation, Jamal Hussain records how the people working on the hub will work together: the days when key people from the web team, Northmere and the wellbeing service meet in person, and the shared online boards that keep each team's work visible to the others. Where should these arrangements be recorded?
o: In the project management team structure.
In the commercial management approach.
In the role descriptions for each team member.
In the quality management approach.
2.w: The project management team structure shows who is involved and how they work together, including working practices that reflect agile and the arrangements for co-located or remote teams, with the tools used for transparency and rich communication (book 7.3.2).

n.1: The commercial management approach covers procurement and the form of contract, such as Northmere's per-iteration payment, not day-to-day working arrangements (book 7.3.2).
n.2: Role descriptions set out each role's specific responsibilities; working practices and co-location arrangements sit in the team structure (book 7.3.2).
n.3: The quality management approach covers quality techniques, standards and responsibilities, including agile testing, not how teams meet and share their work (book 9.3.2).

2.q: During stage 2, Professor Greer and Peter Langley start emailing two web team developers directly with new tasks for the current sprint, including early work on the early-warning feature. The developers begin the work without telling Rebecca Lyle, the web team's product owner. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project executive is accountable for the project and can direct the work of any team member.
Yes, because self-managing developers may take on work from any senior stakeholder who supports the project.
No, because the project manager is the role that should assign each task to the individual developers.
No, because the product owner directs the team's work, so new requests should go through her and the product backlog.
2.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the product owner is a version of the team manager and the only role with direct authority over the delivery team members; the project manager agrees work with the PO as sets of user stories (book 7.3.1). New work should reach the team through the PO's product backlog.

n.0: The executive is accountable for the project, but direct authority over delivery team members sits with the product owner (book 7.3.1).
n.1: Self-management works within the tolerances and work agreed through the product owner, not on requests from any senior stakeholder (book 7.3.1).
n.2: The project manager has direct authority over the product owner, not over individual developers; the PO directs the team (book 7.3.1).

2.q: The Student Support Hub needs a chief product owner to represent its users, who include students and the wellbeing staff who will use the case view, to own the project backlog and to set priorities across the web team and the Northmere team. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to the chief product owner role?
o: Rebecca Lyle, senior digital product manager.
Dr Kwame Mensah, director of student wellbeing.
Maya Kowalczyk, students' union vice-president for welfare.
Professor Alison Greer, pro vice-chancellor.
2.w: The CPO represents the user community, owns the project backlog and sets priorities across teams (book Table 7.2). Kwame Mensah knows students' needs in detail and leads the wellbeing staff who will use the case view, so he can speak for both user groups.

n.0: Rebecca Lyle has managed the web team's backlog for two years, which suits the product owner role for that one team rather than representing users across teams (book Table 7.2).
n.2: Maya Kowalczyk represents students, but not the wellbeing staff who will also use the hub; she is better placed to help recruit and voice the student design panel (book Table 7.2, 4.2.2).
n.3: Professor Greer received the mandate and holds the budget, which fits the project executive role accountable for the project (book Table 7.2).

2.q: The project board wants someone independent of the delivery teams and of the wellbeing service to monitor whether agile practices and governance checks are being followed, and to advise the board and Jamal Hussain on risks, exception reports and their impact on the project canvas. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to the project assurance role?
o: Chloe Hartley, Scrum master for the web team.
Rebecca Lyle, senior digital product manager.
Daniel Ferreira, head of the web team.
Sinead Walsh, quality and enhancement manager.
2.w: Project assurance monitors adherence to PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices, builds quality and governance checks into delivery, and advises the board and project manager on issues, risks, exception reports and impacts on the canvas (book Table 7.2). Sinead Walsh reviews services against standards and is independent of the wellbeing service and the teams.

n.0: Chloe Hartley works inside the web team as its Scrum master, which fits the team coach role; she is not independent of a delivery team (book Table 7.2).
n.1: Rebecca Lyle manages the web team's backlog and fits the product owner role, so she would be assuring her own team's work (book Table 7.2).
n.2: Daniel Ferreira heads the web team that builds the hub, so he is on the supplier side and not independent of the delivery teams (book Table 7.2).

2.q: During initiation, Rebecca Lyle and the web team need to size about 120 user stories for the hub so that Jamal Hussain can draft a first release map. Time is short, and Daniel Ferreira does not want the team to spend days debating each story. Which estimating approach is MOST suitable?
o: Magic estimation, with the whole team quickly placing the stories in order of relative size with little discussion of each.
Ask Daniel Ferreira to estimate all 120 stories himself in story points, so that the developers' time is kept for building.
Use the Northmere team's past velocity to size the web team's stories, as Northmere has delivered similar integration work.
Estimate each story in hours with the most experienced developer, then add up the hours to fix the Release 1 end date.
2.w: Agile estimation is relative and draws on the whole team. Magic estimation is a quick, collaborative technique for early planning that sizes many stories without lengthy discussion (book 8.4.3), which fits sizing 120 stories for a first release map.

n.1: Agile estimates should harness the whole team so that everyone contributes; one person's estimates lose the team's knowledge and shared commitment (book 8.4.3).
n.2: Velocity is a team's rate of delivery used for forecasting, not a way to size stories, and forecasts should use the team's own figures (book 8.3, 12.4.3).
n.3: PRINCE2 Agile uses relative estimates from the whole team, not hour-by-hour estimates from one person, and time is already fixed by Welcome Week (book 8.4.3, Table 3.1).
